power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Background: Young-onset dementia is frequently misdiagnosed, particularly where neurodegenerative and primary psychiatric disorders (PPD) overlap.
Plasma biomarkers measure current pathology, whereas polygenic risk scores (PRS) capture lifelong genetic risk.
Whether PRS derived from late-onset and population samples transfer to young-onset presentations, and how they relate to plasma biomarkers, is unknown.

Methods: We studied 687 participants of European ancestry from the Markers in Neuropsychiatric Disorders (MiND) Study, a prospective young-onset neuropsychiatry cohort: 195 healthy controls (HC), 283 PPD, 55 Alzheimer's disease (AD) and 154 non-AD neurodegenerative disease (oNDG).
PRS for AD, a cross-disorder psychiatric factor (PSY), frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body dementia and Parkinson's disease were computed with PRS-CS, excluding the APOE locus.
Plasma NfL, GFAP and p-tau217 were available for 332 participants.
Models were adjusted for age, sex and APOE ε4 dose.
Results: Relative to HC, the AD PRS was associated with AD (OR 1.69 per SD, 95% CI 1.17-2.45) but not PPD (0.95, 0.77-1.16).
The PSY PRS showed the reciprocal pattern (PPD 1.29, 1.05-1.58; AD 1.00, 0.72-1.40).
No PRS was associated with any plasma protein.
In distinguishing PPD from oNDG, NfL was the strongest discriminator (OR 2.15, 1.62-2.83).
The AD PRS was also associated with oNDG (1.38, 1.11-1.71), without improving discrimination (AUC 0.764 for NfL alone versus 0.773 combined).
Conclusion: In young-onset presentations, AD and psychiatric polygenic risk are disease-specific and independent of plasma biomarkers of neurodegeneration.
Their combined diagnostic value requires evaluation in larger, longitudinal pre-clinical cohorts.

Young-onset dementia, with symptom onset before 65 years, has an estimated global prevalence of 119 per 100,000. 1 It arises from a heterogeneous group of neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's disease (AD), whose early features often overlap with primary psychiatric disorders (PPD). 2 Diagnosis in this age group is often incorrect, necessitating diagnostic revision after further observation and testing. 3 Nearly one-third of individuals with early neurodegenerative disease receive a prior psychiatric diagnosis 4 , and nearly 40% of those presenting with young-onset neurocognitive symptoms have their initial diagnosis revised during follow-up. 5 Time to diagnosis is longer than in late-onset dementia. 6 Plasma biomarkers have begun to address this problem.

text.text: Phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) is highly specific for AD pathology and distinguishes AD from other neurodegenerative disorders, including in a young-onset clinical cohort. [7] [8] [9] Neurofilament light chain (NfL), a non-specific marker of neuroaxonal injury, separates neurodegenerative disorders from PPD. [10] [11] [12] Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), a marker of astrocytic activation and neuroinflammation, has shown less consistent discriminative value. 13 In the Markers in Neuropsychiatric Disorders (MiND) Study, a real-world clinical cohort of young-onset neurocognitive symptoms 14 , plasma p-tau217 distinguished AD from behaviouralvariant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) and from PPD with accuracies of 96% and 93%.

text.text: NfL best separated all neurodegenerative disorders from PPD, while GFAP demonstrated minimal additional value. 15 Nonetheless, nearly half of those with bvFTD had normal p-tau217 and NfL profiles.

text.text: Protein biomarkers therefore leave a proportion of neurodegenerative presentations unresolved.

As measures of current pathology, they also capture dynamic disease state rather than underlying susceptibility. 16 Genetics offer a complementary, static measure of the baseline disease liability. 16 Beyond APOE, the strongest risk factor for AD, successive genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of AD have expanded the number of associated risk loci. [17] [18] [19] Polygenic risk scores (PRS) aggregate these effects into an individual measure of genetic liability.

text.text: GWAS also exist for non-AD causes of dementia including FTD 20 , Lewy body dementia 21 , and Parkinson's disease. 22 These scores are derived predominantly from late-onset or population samples, and their transferability to young-onset clinical presentations is uncertain.

text.text: Some studies support a shared common-variant architecture between late-and early-onset AD [23] [24] [25] , whereas others find little contribution of lateonset polygenic risk. 26, 27 For psychiatric illness, genomic structural equation modelling across 14 childhood-and adult-onset disorders has defined a common genetic factor shared across psychiatric diagnoses. 28 The psychiatric common-factor PRS has not been examined in a dementia diagnostic setting.

text.text: How genetic liability relates to plasma protein markers is also unresolved.
In older and population-based cohorts, the genetic contribution to plasma biomarker levels is carried largely by APOE.

An APOE-excluded AD PRS showed no association with p-tau217, Aβ42/40, NfL or GFAP across ages 30-80 29 , and associations elsewhere have been confined to specific subgroups or outcomes. 30, 31 Combined genetic risk scores and plasma biomarkers appear to carry partly distinct information in late-onset dementia. 32, 33 Whether genetic and protein markers are independent in a young-onset population, and whether this extends to psychiatric liability, is unknown.

text.text: We aimed to address these gaps through analysis of a prospective cohort of patients referred to a tertiary young-onset neuropsychiatry service.
In this study, we set out to test whether diseasespecific PRS mark their corresponding clinical diagnoses and are independent of plasma NfL, GFAP and p-tau217.
We also tested whether NfL and AD PRS contribute independently to distinguishing PPD from non-AD neurodegeneration, a common and challenging clinical scenario.

Participants with young-onset neurocognitive and psychiatric symptoms referred to a tertiary center for diagnostic work-up were prospectively recruited for the MiND Study. 3, 11, 12, 15 After a follow-up period of over one year, a diagnosis was determined using consensus criteria, with details published prior. 15 This study, part of the Markers in Neuropsychiatric Disorders Study (The MiND Study), was approved by the Melbourne Health Human Research Ethics Committee (2016.038, 2017.090, 2018.371, 2020.142) and the Walter and Eliza Hall Institute Human Research Ethics Committee (project ID 23/27).

text.text: For each trait, the effective sample size reported in the original GWAS was supplied as the PRS-CS N. Posterior SNP weights were estimated per chromosome (1-22) against the 1000 Genomes European LD reference, with the global shrinkage parameter learned from the data (PRS-CS auto).
Per-chromosome posterior weights were concatenated and scores computed in the TOPMed-imputed, quality-controlled MiND participants genotypes with PLINK 2.0 using allele-matched effect sizes.

PRS were calculated using summary statistics for AD [17] [18] [19] , PSY (cross-disorders P-factor) 28 , FTD 20 , LBD 21 , and PD. 22 Each score was adjusted for residual population structure by regression on the first ten genetic principal components, and the residuals standardised to mean 0 and standard deviation (SD) 1 in healthy controls.

text.text: Analyses were performed in R 4.5.3 and were restricted to the European-ancestry subset.
Tests were two-sided with a nominal significance threshold of 0.05.
We distinguish nominal p-values (p nom ) from Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate-adjusted p-values (p adj ) throughout.

Falsediscovery-rate correction was applied within pre-specified families: for each biomarker or polygenic risk score (PRS), the family comprised its three group contrasts against healthy controls (HC) within a given covariate set; for the primary psychiatric disorder (PPD) versus non-AD neurodegenerative disease (oNDG) univariate analysis, the family comprised the candidate predictors within a covariate set.
Each PRS was expressed in SD units of the European-ancestry HC distribution.

Plasma biomarkers were natural-log-transformed and expressed as z-scores relative to the Europeanancestry HC mean and SD; untransformed concentrations (pg/mL) were used for descriptive summaries and figures.
Unless stated otherwise, models were adjusted for age at blood draw, sex, and APOE ε4 allele dose.
Descriptive statistics are medians (interquartile range) for continuous variables and counts (percentages) for categorical variables.

Unadjusted differences across the four diagnostic groups were tested by the Kruskal-Wallis test for continuous variables (age) and the Pearson chi-square test for categorical variables (sex, APOE ε4 carriership).
Availability of the plasma panel by diagnostic group was compared by chi-square test.

Five candidate AD PRS [17] [18] [19] builds were compared for their discrimination of AD from HC by logistic regression (odds ratio [OR] per SD, adjusted for age, sex, and APOE ε4 dose, with Wald 95% confidence intervals [CIs]).

Condition specificity of the AD and psychiatric (PSY) 28 genetic-liability axes was assessed in four separate two-group logistic models, pairing each score (AD PRS, PSY PRS) with each contrast (AD versus HC, PPD versus HC), each fitted on its own complete-case sample and adjusted for covariates.

text.text: Each model consisted of the OR per SD (Wald 95% CI), the apparent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of the PRS-plus-covariate model with DeLong 95% CIs, and the apparent AUC of a covariate-only model.
Plasma NfL, GFAP, and p-tau217 concentrations were summarised by diagnostic group as medians (interquartile range) on the untransformed (pg/mL) scale.
Pairwise associations among the three plasma proteins and five disease PRS were assessed by partial Spearman correlation, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction applied within each matrix.
Two complete-case cohorts were defined.
In the maximum-n cohort, each predictor was modelled in the largest sample that supported it (genotype for PRS, the relevant assay for protein biomarkers).
The primary cohort was complete on the pre-specified predictors (NfL and AD PRS) and covariates; the joint model and all discrimination statistics were fitted to this cohort.
Each predictor was first tested univariately by logistic regression (OR per SD, adjusted for covariates), in both cohorts.
The joint multivariable model entered NfL and AD PRS simultaneously together with covariates, allowing each marker to be assessed adjusted for the other.

Discrimination was summarised by the AUC of four nested models (covariates only; NfL; AD PRS; NfL plus AD PRS): apparent AUCs are shown, and both apparent and optimismcorrected AUCs (Harrell bootstrap, 1000 resamples, non-converged resamples excluded) were calculated.

text.text: AD PRS discriminated AD from HC (OR 1.69 per SD [95% CI: 1.17 -2.45], p nom = 0.005) but not PPD from HC (OR 0.95 [95% CI: 0.77 -1.16], p nom = 0.60), whereas PSY PRS discriminated PPD from HC (OR 1.29 [95% CI: 1.05 -1.58], p nom = 0.013) but not AD from HC (OR 1.00 [95% CI: 0.72 -1.40], p nom = 0.99); neither PRS was associated with the other diagnostic group.

Similarly, relative to a model with age, sex, and APOE ε4 dose alone, each PRS improved the AUC only for its own contrast and by a small margin (AD PRS in AD, 0.73 to 0.76; PSY PRS in PPD, 0.70 to 0.71), while the contrasting-comparison AUCs were unchanged (0.73 and 0.70).
The genetic associations were therefore condition-specific but added little discrimination beyond demographic covariates.

We next examined whether the genetic and protein biomarkers were correlated.

After adjusting for age, sex, APOE ε4 dose, and diagnosis, the only associations to survive correction were among the three protein markers (NfL-GFAP ρ = 0.40, GFAP-p-tau217 ρ = 0.32, NfL-p-tau217 ρ = 0.25; all p adj < 10 ), with one weak correlation between AD PRS and FTD PRS (ρ = 0.10, p adj = 0.043) (Supplementary Figures 4 and 5, Supplementary Table 7).

text.text: Within this cohort, the disease genetic liability captured by the PRS and the protein biomarker levels were statistically independent.
A diagnostic challenge in young-onset presentations is separating PPD from non-AD neurodegeneration, where symptoms often overlap.
We used this clinical dilemma as motivation to determine the contributions of protein and genetic biomarkers in differentiating between these two clinically-ambiguous conditions.
Univariate and multivariable analyses demonstrated that both NfL levels and AD PRS were independent discriminators of PPD from oNDG.

NfL provided the strongest separation with univariate analysis (OR 2.15 per SD [1.62 -2.83], p nom = 7.5 × 10 , p adj = 6.0 × 10 7 ; adjusted for age, sex, and APOE ε4 dose; Figure 3A, Supplementary Table 9).

text.text: We examined disease-specific genetic liability alongside plasma NfL, GFAP and p-tau217 in a real-world young-onset dementia cohort and observed three main findings.
First, genetic liability to AD and to PPD were distinct.

The AD PRS 19 was associated with AD but not PPD relative to HC, and the psychiatric common-factor PRS 28 (which represents the shared genetic architecture amongst psychiatric diseases) showed the reciprocal pattern.
text.formatted: The AD PRS <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> was associated with AD but not PPD relative to HC, and the psychiatric common-factor PRS <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> (which represents the shared genetic architecture amongst psychiatric diseases) showed the reciprocal pattern.

text.text: Second, genetic liability was statistically independent of plasma protein levels as the only significant correlations were among the proteins themselves.
Third, in separating PPD from non-AD neurodegeneration, NfL was the dominant discriminator, and the AD PRS carried a small, but independent association.

Together, these results indicate that genetic liability and plasma protein markers capture separable dimensions of disease, even in a diagnostically heterogeneous young-onset population where misdiagnosis and diagnostic delay are most common.

text.text: These findings are consistent with a shared common-variant architecture between late-onset and young-onset AD 23 , and with studies showing that late-onset AD PRS carry signal in younger cases. 24, 25, 45 Transferability has not been uniform, however, with some studies finding little contribution of late-onset polygenic risk to early-onset or atypical AD. 26, 27, 46 Further work, with increased cohort size, is needed to more precisely understand the genetic contribution of lateonset AD genetic liability in young-onset cases.

text.text: The association of the psychiatric common-factor PRS with PPD is, to our knowledge, the first demonstration of psychiatric genetic risk in a young-onset dementia diagnostic setting.

The PSY PRS, derived from genomic structural equation modelling across 14 psychiatric disorders 28 , was associated with PPD relative to HC (OR 1.29 per SD) and showed no association with AD (OR 1.00).

text.text: These findings suggest that a cross-disorder factor is applicable to a clinical PPD group that spans depressive, bipolar, psychotic and functional presentations.
The reciprocal pattern is informative in both directions.
Patients whose presentations were ultimately attributed to a psychiatric cause carried the polygenic signature of psychiatric illness.
They did not carry excess AD liability (-0.05 SD relative to HC), in keeping with their low p-tau217 levels.

The PSY PRS did not significantly discriminate between PPD and oNDG, a common clinical challenge (OR 0.88 [95% CI 0.71 -1.09], Supplementary Table 10 for the full genotyped cohort). oNDG was intermediate between HC and PPD on the PSY PRS axis (+0.14 SD relative to HC), so the two groups differed by only 0.11 SD.

text.text: The oNDG group also reflects the referral pattern of a tertiary neuropsychiatry service, with substantial representation of Huntington's disease and heterogeneous non-AD dementias, and its psychiatric genetic liability may not generalise to neurodegenerative cohorts of different composition.
Larger studies with adequately sized, diagnostically defined neurodegenerative groups are needed to establish whether psychiatric polygenic liability contributes to this distinction.

Behavioural-variant FTD should be a priority, as a frequent mimic of primary psychiatric disorders, especially when NfL plasma levels may be in the normal range. 15 The disease-PRS we tested were not associated with plasma protein levels.

text.text: Independence also implies that genetic and protein measures carry complementary information.

Utility of these orthogonal signals is not clearly demonstrated in our or other's work; how these signals can be exploited to obtain earlier and more accurate diagnoses, especially in prodromal or preclinical states remains to be determined.
The comparison of PPD with non-AD neurodegeneration was used to test independence directly, in the clinical contrast where symptoms most often overlap.

text.text: It retained this association when modelled jointly with NfL, while discrimination changed little (AUC 0.764 for NfL, 0.773 combined).
With orthogonal predictors and a much stronger protein marker, this non-additivity is not surprising.
It confirms that the AD PRS carries information distinct from NfL that does not improve discrimination in clinically established cases.
This supports further research into the utility of PRS prior to clinical diagnoses in a real-world clinical cohort.
This study has several limitations.
Genotyping platform was aligned with diagnosis as AD participants underwent WGS, HC and PPD participants were array-genotyped, and oNDG participants were split across platforms.
We mitigated this by restricting sequencing data to array sites before joint imputation.
The null PSY, FTD, LBD and PD PRS contrasts between AD and HC also act as internal negative controls.
Residual platform effects nevertheless cannot be fully excluded.
The oNDG group reflects the referral pattern of the Royal Melbourne Hospital Neuropsychiatry Centre.
It over-represents Huntington's disease, with few FTD, LBD and PD cases, which limits power for the corresponding disease-specific PRS and generalisability to general memory clinics.
The association of the AD PRS with oNDG may partly reflect AD copathology or unrecognised AD within oNDG, particularly as diagnoses were clinical and not all participants had CSF or PET confirmation.
The AD PRS build was selected on the AD-versus-HC contrast, so the reported OR is likely optimistic, although all three Consensus builds gave overlapping estimates.
The plasma panel was available for 48% of the cohort and less often in PPD (29%), so the primary PPD-versus-oNDG cohort was a selected subset.
The AD PRS estimate was nevertheless the same in this subset and in the full genotyped cohort (OR 1.38 per SD in both).
The AD group was modest (n = 55), and the design was cross-sectional so biomarker levels may be impacted by dementia severity in addition to the underlying pathology.
Analyses were restricted to European ancestry, thereby limiting PRS effect generalizability to other ancestral groups.

In summary, in a young-onset neuropsychiatry cohort, AD and psychiatric genetic liability each marked its own condition relative to healthy controls, and both were independent of plasma biomarkers of neurodegeneration.
Genetic liability and protein biomarkers capture distinct dimensions of disease.
Establishing whether this complementary structure translates into diagnostic benefit will require external validation, longitudinal follow-up with prodromal cases, and multi-ancestry cohorts.
